subject: math
title: Grade 6 Triangles: Classify by Sides and Angles, Angle Sum and Missing Angles
seo_title: Grade 6 Triangles Worksheets: Classify Triangles and Find Missing Angles (Free Math, Answer Key, BC Curriculum)
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 math worksheets on triangles for the BC curriculum: classify triangles as equilateral, isosceles or scalene and as acute, right or obtuse, use the 180° angle sum, find missing angles in isosceles and right triangles, and solve word problems about yield signs, roofs and sails. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Name a triangle by its sides and by its largest angle. Its 3 angles always add to 180°.
key_sub: Equilateral, isosceles, scalene: count the equal sides. Acute, right, obtuse: look at the largest angle. Missing angle: subtract the two known angles from 180°. A right triangle has only 1 right angle.
body_html:
Name a triangle by its sides

Look at the sides. Tick marks show sides that are equal.

NameSides
Equilateralall 3 sides equal
Isosceles2 sides equal
Scaleneno sides equal

Name a triangle by its angles

Look at the largest angle. A right angle is exactly 90°. A small square marks it.

NameAngles
Acuteall 3 angles less than 90°
Rightone angle exactly 90°
Obtuseone angle more than 90°

A triangle can have both names. A triangle with a right angle and 2 equal sides is a right isosceles triangle.

Example 1

A triangle has sides of 6 cm, 6 cm and 4 cm, and angles of 70°, 70° and 40°. Name it.

Two sides are equal: isosceles. All angles are less than 90°: acute.

Answer: an acute isosceles triangle

The angles add to 180°

The 3 angles of every triangle add to 180°, big or small. Tear off the 3 corners of a paper triangle and they make a straight line.

To find a missing angle, add the two you know and subtract from 180°.

Example 2

Two angles of a triangle are 52.5° and 74.5°. Find the third angle.

52.5° + 74.5° = 127°. 180° − 127° = 53°.

Answer: 53°

Isosceles and right triangles

In an isosceles triangle, the 2 angles next to the third side are equal. In a right triangle, the other 2 angles add to 90°.

Example 3

The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. Find the angles.

1 + 2 + 3 = 6 parts. 180° ÷ 6 = 30° per part. The angles are 30°, 60° and 90°.

Answer: 30°, 60° and 90° (a right triangle)

Construct a triangle. Draw one side with a ruler. Use a protractor to draw the angle at each end. The two new lines meet at the third corner. A 6 cm side with 60° at both ends makes an equilateral triangle.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
A right triangle has 2 right anglesIt has exactly 1. The other 2 angles are acute and add to 90°
An isosceles triangle must point upCount the equal sides. It can point any way
A triangle with 2 acute angles is acuteEvery triangle has 2 acute angles. Look at the largest one
Subtracting from 360° or 90°The angles of a triangle add to 180°
Subtracting only one known angleSubtract both known angles from 180°
Forgetting to halve for 2 equal anglesSubtract the top angle from 180°, then divide by 2
A bigger triangle has bigger angles in totalEvery triangle’s angles add to 180°

faq.q: What do Grade 6 students learn about triangles in the BC math curriculum?
faq.a: In Geometry and measurement, Grade 6 students classify triangles by their sides and by their angles, learn that the 3 angles add to 180°, and use this to find missing angles and construct triangles.

faq.q: Do the angles of a triangle always add up to 180°?
faq.a: Yes. In every triangle the 3 angles add to 180°, no matter how big it is. To find a missing angle, add the two known angles and subtract from 180°.

faq.q: Can a triangle have two right angles?
faq.a: No. Two right angles already make 180°, so nothing is left for the third angle. A right triangle has exactly 1 right angle and 2 acute angles.

faq.q: How do you find the missing angles of an isosceles triangle?
faq.a: The 2 base angles are equal. If you know the top angle, subtract it from 180° and divide by 2. If you know one base angle, double it and subtract from 180°.

items.q: Classify this triangle by its sides. Use the tick marks.
items.e: No two sides are equal, so it is a scalene triangle. There are no tick marks, so all 3 sides are different lengths.

items.q: Which triangle is isosceles?
items.e: Triangle A has tick marks on 2 sides, so it is isosceles, even though it points down. The other triangles have no equal sides.

items.q: Which triangle is equilateral?
items.e: Triangle D has tick marks on all 3 sides. The upright triangle has only 2 equal sides, so it is isosceles.

items.q: Owen says a triangle can only be isosceles if it points up. Is he right?
c: No, it can point any way
items.e: The name depends only on the sides. Turning an isosceles triangle does not change its 2 equal sides.

items.q: Classify this triangle by its sides.
items.e: Exactly 2 sides are equal, so it is an isosceles triangle. Two sides are 7.5 cm. It points down, but it is still isosceles.

items.q: Classify this triangle by its sides.
items.e: Exactly 2 sides are equal, so it is an isosceles triangle. Two sides are 6 cm, so exactly 2 sides are equal. The equal sides do not have to be the slanted ones.

items.q: Classify this triangle by its sides. Use the tick marks.
items.e: No two sides are equal, so it is a scalene triangle. There are no tick marks, so no two sides are equal.

items.q: Classify this triangle by its sides. Use the tick marks.
items.e: All 3 sides are equal, so it is an equilateral triangle. The tick marks show 3 equal sides. Pointing down does not change the name.

items.q: Classify this triangle by its sides. Use the tick marks.
items.e: Exactly 2 sides are equal, so it is an isosceles triangle. It lies on its side, but 2 sides still have tick marks. An isosceles triangle can point in any direction.

items.q: An isosceles triangle has two sides of 7 cm and one side of 4 cm. What is its perimeter?
items.e: Add all 3 sides: 7 + 7 + 4 = 18 cm. (11 cm forgets one of the 7 cm sides.)

items.q: Classify this triangle by its sides.
items.e: No two sides are equal, so it is a scalene triangle. The sides are 9 cm, 6 cm and 5 cm. All 3 are different.

items.q: An equilateral triangle has a perimeter of 36 cm. How long is each side?
items.e: All 3 sides are equal: 36 ÷ 3 = 12 cm. (18 cm is 36 ÷ 2 and 9 cm is 36 ÷ 4.)

items.q: Classify this triangle by its sides.
items.e: No two sides are equal, so it is a scalene triangle. The sides are 4 cm, 3 cm and 5 cm, all different. (It is also a right triangle, but that is a name by angles.)

items.q: Which triangle is scalene?
items.e: Triangle C has no tick marks, so no two sides are equal. The others have 2 or 3 equal sides.

items.q: Classify this triangle by its sides. Use the tick marks.
items.e: Exactly 2 sides are equal, so it is an isosceles triangle. An isosceles triangle can point down. Turning a triangle never changes its name.

items.q: A triangle has sides of 5 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm. Classify it by its sides.
items.e: Two sides are 5 cm, so exactly 2 sides are equal: isosceles.

items.q: Classify this triangle by its sides.
items.e: All 3 sides are equal, so it is an equilateral triangle. All 3 sides are 8 cm.

items.q: A triangle has sides of 4.5 cm, 6 cm and 7.5 cm. Classify it by its sides.
items.e: 4.5 cm, 6 cm and 7.5 cm are all different, so the triangle is scalene.

items.q: Classify this triangle by its sides. Use the tick marks.
items.e: Exactly 2 sides are equal, so it is an isosceles triangle. The 2 slanted sides have tick marks, and the base has none.

items.q: Classify this triangle by its sides. Use the tick marks.
items.e: Exactly 2 sides are equal, so it is an isosceles triangle. The 2 sides next to the right angle have tick marks. Turned or not, it is isosceles.

items.q: Name this triangle by its angles and its sides.
items.e: One angle is exactly 90°, so it is a right triangle. Exactly 2 sides are equal, so it is an isosceles triangle. Its full name is right isosceles triangle.

items.q: Every triangle has at least how many acute angles?
items.e: A triangle can have at most 1 angle that is 90° or more. So at least 2 of its 3 angles are acute.

items.q: Classify this triangle by its angles.
items.e: All 3 angles are less than 90°, so it is an acute triangle. 75°, 60° and 45° are all less than 90°.

items.q: Classify this triangle by its angles.
items.e: One angle is more than 90°, so it is an obtuse triangle. 110° is more than 90°. Pointing down does not change the name.

items.q: Classify this triangle by its angles.
items.e: All 3 angles are less than 90°, so it is an acute triangle. 60°, 50° and 70° are all less than 90°.

items.q: What is the greatest number of right angles a triangle can have?
items.e: Two right angles already make 90° + 90° = 180°, and that leaves 0° for the third angle. So a triangle has at most 1 right angle.

items.q: A triangle has angles of 60°, 60° and 60°. Classify it by its angles.
items.e: All 3 angles are 60°, less than 90°, so it is acute. (It is also equilateral, but that is a name by sides.)

items.q: Which triangle is a right triangle?
items.e: Triangle B has a small square in one corner, so one angle is 90°. It is turned, but it is still a right triangle.

items.q: Emma draws a right triangle. She says it has 2 right angles, at the bottom corners. Is she right?
items.e: A right triangle has exactly 1 right angle. The other 2 angles are acute and add up to 90°.

items.q: Can a triangle have 2 obtuse angles?
items.e: Two obtuse angles are each more than 90°, so together they are more than 180°. The 3 angles of a triangle add to only 180°.

items.q: Classify this triangle by its angles.
items.e: One angle is exactly 90°, so it is a right triangle. The small square shows a 90° angle. The triangle is turned, but it is still a right triangle.

items.q: A triangle has angles of 100°, 40° and 40°. Classify it by its angles.
items.e: 100° is more than 90°, so it is obtuse. Two acute angles do not make it acute: every triangle has at least 2.

items.q: Classify this triangle by its angles.
items.e: One angle is more than 90°, so it is an obtuse triangle. 100° is more than 90°. It has 2 acute angles too, but a triangle is named by its largest angle.

items.q: Classify this triangle by its angles.
items.e: One angle is exactly 90°, so it is a right triangle. The small square shows a 90° angle. The other two angles, 40° and 50°, are acute.

items.q: A triangle has angles of 90°, 45° and 45°. Classify it by its angles.
items.e: One angle is exactly 90°, so it is a right triangle.

items.q: Name this triangle by its angles and its sides.
items.e: One angle is wider than a right angle, so it is obtuse. Exactly 2 sides are equal, so it is an isosceles triangle. Its full name is obtuse isosceles triangle.

items.q: A triangle has angles of 88°, 47° and 45°. Classify it by its angles.
items.e: 88° is close to 90°, but it is still less than 90°. All 3 angles are acute.

items.q: Name this triangle by its angles and its sides.
items.e: One angle is wider than a right angle, so it is obtuse. No two sides are equal, so it is a scalene triangle. Its full name is obtuse scalene triangle.

items.q: Which triangle is obtuse?
items.e: Triangle C has one wide angle, more than 90°. The right triangle has a 90° angle, and the other two have only acute angles.

items.q: Name this triangle by its angles and its sides.
items.e: No angle is 90° or wider, so it is acute. Exactly 2 sides are equal, so it is an isosceles triangle. Its full name is acute isosceles triangle.

sets.title: The angles of a triangle add to 180°

items.q: Ji-woo measures the angles of a triangle as 62°, 58° and 70°. What can you say?
items.e: 62 + 58 + 70 = 190. The angles of a triangle must add to exactly 180°, so at least one measurement is wrong.

items.q: Two angles of a triangle are 50° and 60°. Classify the triangle by its angles.
items.e: First find the third angle: 180° − 50° − 60° = 70°. All 3 angles (50°, 60° and 70°) are less than 90°, so it is acute.

items.q: Chloe tears off the 3 corners of a paper triangle and puts them together, point to point. What do they make?
items.e: The 3 angles of a triangle add to 180°, so the corners fit together to make a straight line.

items.q: Two angles of a triangle add to less than 90°. What kind of triangle is it?
items.e: The third angle is 180° minus a number less than 90°, so it is more than 90°. The triangle is obtuse.

items.q: Which three angles could be the angles of a right triangle?
items.e: 25 + 65 + 90 = 180, so these angles work. The others do not add to 180°: 25°, 75°, 90° adds to 190°, 30°, 50°, 90° adds to 170°, 45°, 45°, 100° adds to 190°.

items.q: Two angles of a triangle add to 90°. What is the third angle?
items.e: 180° − 90° = 90°. The third angle is a right angle.

items.q: Which three angles could be the angles of an isosceles triangle?
items.e: 110 + 35 + 35 = 180, so these angles work. The others do not add to 180°: 110°, 40°, 40° adds to 190°, 100°, 35°, 35° adds to 170°, 70°, 70°, 50° adds to 190°.

items.q: What is the size of each angle in an equilateral triangle?
items.e: The 3 angles are equal and add to 180°: 180° ÷ 3 = 60°. (120° comes from dividing 360° by 3.)

items.q: One angle of a triangle is 100°. What do the other two angles add up to?
items.e: 180° − 100° = 80°. (260° subtracts from 360°, and 40° is half of 80°: that is only one angle if they are equal.)

items.q: The two acute angles of a right triangle add up to what?
items.e: All 3 angles add to 180°, and the right angle uses 90°. 180° − 90° = 90° is left for the other two.

items.q: Which three angles could be the angles of a triangle?
items.e: 50 + 60 + 70 = 180, so these angles work. The others do not add to 180°: 50°, 60°, 80° adds to 190°, 90°, 45°, 55° adds to 190°, 100°, 50°, 40° adds to 190°.

items.q: One angle of a triangle is 120°. What are the other two angles like?
items.e: 180° − 120° = 60° is left for the other two angles. Each one is less than 60°, so both are acute.

items.q: The 3 angles of any triangle add up to what?
items.e: The angles of every triangle add to 180°. (360° is the total for a square or any four-sided shape.)

items.q: Two angles of a triangle are 35° and 55°. Classify the triangle by its angles.
items.e: First find the third angle: 180° − 35° − 55° = 90°. 90° is a right angle, so it is a right triangle. Both given angles are acute, but the third one decides.

items.q: Ryan draws a big triangle and a small triangle. He says the angles of the big one add to more than 180°. Is he right?
items.e: The angles of every triangle add to 180°, big or small. A bigger triangle has longer sides, not bigger angles in total.

items.q: Two angles of a triangle are 65° and 70°. Classify the triangle by its angles.
items.e: First find the third angle: 180° − 65° − 70° = 45°. All 3 angles (65°, 70° and 45°) are less than 90°, so it is acute.

items.q: Two angles of a triangle are 44° and 46°. Classify the triangle by its angles.
items.e: First find the third angle: 180° − 44° − 46° = 90°. 90° is a right angle, so it is a right triangle. Both given angles are acute, but the third one decides.

items.q: Which set of angles can make a triangle?
items.e: 30 + 60 + 90 = 180, so these angles work. The others do not add to 180°: 30°, 60°, 100° adds to 190°, 45°, 45°, 45° adds to 135°, 120°, 30°, 40° adds to 190°.

items.q: Two angles of a triangle are 25° and 40°. Classify the triangle by its angles.
items.e: First find the third angle: 180° − 25° − 40° = 115°. 115° is more than 90°, so it is obtuse. Both given angles are acute, but the third one decides.

items.q: Mei measures two angles of a triangle: 95° and 85°. Is this possible?
items.e: 95° + 85° = 180°, which leaves 0° for the third angle. A triangle needs 3 angles, so this is not possible.

items.q: Two angles of a triangle are 47° and 68°. What is the third angle?
Find the size of the angle marked “?”.
In triangle PQR, angle P is 38°. Angle Q is 2 times angle P. What is angle R?
items.e: Angle Q = 2 × 38° = 76°. Angle R = 180° − 38° − 76° = 66°. (76° is angle Q, not angle R.)

items.q: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. What is the largest angle?
items.e: There are 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 parts. 180° ÷ 6 = 30° per part. The largest angle is 3 × 30° = 90°. (30° is one part only.)

items.q: A right triangle has two acute angles. One is 2 times the other. What are the two acute angles?
items.e: The acute angles add to 90°. Split 90° into 3 equal parts: 90° ÷ 3 = 30°. So the angles are 30° and 2 × 30° = 60°.

items.q: A right triangle has two equal angles. How big is each equal angle?
items.e: The right angle is 90°, so the other two add to 180° − 90° = 90°. 90° ÷ 2 = 45°.

items.q: Find the size of the angle marked “?”.
items.e: The tick marks show an isosceles triangle, so the 2 bottom angles are equal: both are 70°. 180° − 70° − 70° = 40°.

items.q: The top angle of an isosceles triangle is 40°. The other 2 angles are equal. How big is each one?
items.e: 180° − 40° = 140° is shared by 2 equal angles: 140° ÷ 2 = 70°. (140° forgets to halve.)

items.q: Nadia writes the equation a + 115 = 180 to find a missing angle a. What is a?
items.e: Subtract to undo the addition: a = 180 − 115 = 65. So a = 65°. (295° adds instead of subtracting.)

items.q: A right triangle has one angle of 25°. What is the third angle?
items.e: The right angle is 90°. 180° − 90° − 25° = 65°. (155° forgets the right angle.)

items.q: Find the size of the angle marked “?”.
Find the size of the angle marked “?”.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add to 180°. 50° + 60° = 110°, and 180° − 110° = 70°.

items.q: An obtuse isosceles triangle has a 120° angle. The other 2 angles are equal. How big is each one?
items.e: 180° − 120° = 60°, shared by 2 equal angles: 60° ÷ 2 = 30°. (60° forgets to halve; 120° subtracts from 360°.)

items.q: Find the size of the angle marked “?”.
items.e: The tick marks show an isosceles triangle, so the 2 angles next to the unmarked side are equal. 180° − 50° = 130°, and 130° ÷ 2 = 65°.

items.q: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles of 72.5°. What is the third angle?
items.e: 72.5° + 72.5° = 145°. 180° − 145° = 35°. (107.5° subtracts only one of the equal angles.)

items.q: Find the size of the angle marked “?”.
items.e: 45° + 105° = 150°, and 180° − 150° = 30°. Turning the triangle does not change its angles.

items.q: Find the size of the angle marked “?”.
items.e: The small square is 90°. 180° − 90° − 38° = 52°. (142° forgets the right angle.)

items.q: Two angles of a triangle are 52.5° and 74.5°. What is the third angle?
items.e: 52.5° + 74.5° = 127°. 180° − 127° = 53°. (63° is a subtraction slip, and 127° is the sum, not the answer.)

items.q: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles of 35°. What is the third angle?
Find the size of the angle marked “?”.
Kai draws a 6 cm line. At each end he draws a 60° angle, and the two new lines meet. What kind of triangle is it?
items.e: The third angle is 180° − 60° − 60° = 60°. All 3 angles are equal, so all 3 sides are equal (6 cm each).

items.q: A ramp at the school entrance makes a right triangle with the ground. The ramp makes a 5° angle with the ground. What is the third angle?
items.e: 180° − 90° − 5° = 85°. (175° forgets the right angle.)

items.q: Jasleen sews 12 triangle patches for a quilt. Each patch has sides of 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm. How much trim does she need to go around all 12 patches?
items.e: One patch: 6 + 8 + 10 = 24 cm. For 12 patches: 12 × 24 = 288 cm. (24 cm is only one patch, and 120 cm is 12 × 10.)

items.q: The two equal legs of a sign at a farmers’ market in Kelowna meet at the top at 50°. What angle does each leg make with the ground?
items.e: The legs and the ground make an isosceles triangle. 180° − 50° = 130°, and 130° ÷ 2 = 65°.

items.q: A sailboat on English Bay has a triangular sail with a right angle at the bottom. One other angle is 52°. What is the third angle?
items.e: 180° − 90° − 52° = 38°. (128° forgets the right angle.)

items.q: Emma cuts a square Nanaimo bar from corner to corner. What kind of triangles does she get?
items.e: Each piece has a square corner (90°) and 2 equal sides (two sides of the square), so it is a right isosceles triangle.

items.q: Hana cuts a rectangular sheet of paper from corner to corner. One angle in each piece is 35°. What are the other two angles?
items.e: Cutting a rectangle corner to corner keeps a square corner, so one angle is 90°. 180° − 90° − 35° = 55°.

items.q: A bike frame has a triangle with angles of 60° and 70°. What is the third angle?
Liam’s lacrosse team makes a pennant shaped like an isosceles triangle. The pointed end has a 30° angle. The other 2 angles are equal. How big is each one?
items.e: 180° − 30° = 150°, shared by 2 equal angles: 150° ÷ 2 = 75°.

items.q: A garden bed in Surrey is a triangle with sides of 3 m, 4 m and 5 m. Edging costs $8 per metre. How much does edging for the whole bed cost?
items.e: Perimeter: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 m. Cost: 12 × $8 = $96. (12 is the length in metres, not the cost, and $40 is the longest side only.)

items.q: A ladder leans against a wall. The wall meets the ground at a right angle, and the ladder makes a 70° angle with the ground. What angle does the ladder make with the wall?
items.e: The ladder, wall and ground make a right triangle. 180° − 90° − 70° = 20°.

items.q: The roof of a cabin in Whistler makes an isosceles triangle. The two bottom angles are 35° each. What is the angle at the top?
items.e: 35° + 35° = 70°. 180° − 70° = 110°. That angle is more than 90°, so the roof triangle is obtuse.

items.q: A ferry route in BC makes a triangle between three islands. Two of its angles are 40° and 65°. What is the third angle?
Ava says a triangle can have one right angle and one obtuse angle. Is she right?
items.e: 90° plus an angle bigger than 90° is already more than 180°, but all 3 angles must add to 180°.

items.q: Zara draws an 8 cm line. She draws a 90° angle at one end and a 45° angle at the other. What is the third angle?
items.e: 180° − 90° − 45° = 45°. Two equal angles mean two equal sides, so Zara drew a right isosceles triangle.

items.q: Students make triangle flags for the Terry Fox Run. Each flag has angles of 40°, 70° and 70°. What is the full name of the triangle?
items.e: All angles are less than 90° (acute), and 2 equal angles mean 2 equal sides (isosceles).

items.q: On a camping trip in the Okanagan, the front of a tent is an isosceles triangle with sides of 1.5 m, 1.5 m and 2 m. What is its perimeter?
items.e: 1.5 + 1.5 + 2 = 5 m. (3.5 m forgets one of the 1.5 m sides.)

items.q: A yield sign is an equilateral triangle that points down. One yield sign has sides of 75 cm. What is its perimeter?
items.e: All 3 sides are 75 cm: 3 × 75 = 225 cm. (150 cm counts only 2 sides.)

items.q: Simran has straws that are 3 cm, 4 cm and 9 cm long. Can she join their ends to make a triangle?
items.e: The two short straws together are only 7 cm. They cannot reach across the 9 cm straw, so no triangle is made.

items.q: Owen’s class builds a triangular kite frame with angles in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. What is the smallest angle?
items.e: There are 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 parts. 180° ÷ 9 = 20° per part. The smallest angle is 2 × 20° = 40°. (20° is one part only.)
